strengths: Practical problem formulation: The paper tackles a realistic challenge in video anomaly detection (VAD)—the scarcity and cost of acquiring real abnormal surveillance footage—by training an anomaly detector purely on real normal videos paired with diffusion-synthesized pseudo-abnormal videos.

Insightful observation of pseudo-anomaly bias: The discovery that diffusion-synthesized videos exhibit a spatiotemporal magnitude bias (inflated feature norms), which can dominate MIL Top-k selection and cause shortcut learning, is well-demonstrated and practically valuable for the community.

Well-motivated technical design: Both CA-PAG (combining CLIP-guided seed retrieval and VLM prompt refinement) and DARM (combining normal domain alignment with usage-aware prototype memory updates) specifically address the pitfalls of video synthesis and pseudo-supervision.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across three major benchmarks (ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, XD-Violence) as well as open-set anomaly detection settings. Detailed ablations (Table 5a, Table 5b, Table 6) isolate the impact of seed selection, prompt refinement, domain alignment, and usage-aware memory updates.
weaknesses: Feature backbone comparability: The main comparisons in Table 4 evaluate PA-VAD using strong modern multimodal representations (Qwen2.5-VL, 3,584-D), whereas most prior UVAD and WVAD baselines rely on older backbones such as I3D or C3D. Although the authors ablate different detector heads (Sultani, UR-DMU, DARM) under the same Qwen2.5-VL features, evaluating PA-VAD on standard I3D features or testing baseline methods with Qwen2.5-VL features would provide a more rigorous apples-to-apples comparison.

Level of supervision nuances: While PA-VAD does not use real abnormal videos, it requires predefined abnormal class category names/metadata and powerful pretrained foundational models (Wan 2.2, Qwen3, CLIP). In contrast, standard UVAD assumes zero knowledge about potential anomaly categories. Although open-set experiments partially alleviate this concern, the distinction between true unsupervised setups and text-guided pseudo supervision should be characterized with even greater nuance.

High computational generation cost: The video synthesis step requires substantial offline resources (e.g., Wan 2.2 takes ~9.5 minutes per clip on dual RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, totaling ~55 hours for UCF-Crime), which somewhat dampens the claim of zero-cost data collection.

strengths: Practical and timely research direction: replacing scarce, privacy-sensitive, and difficult-to-collect real abnormal videos with diffusion-generated pseudo-anomalies while achieving competitive or superior performance to methods trained on real abnormal footage.

Insightful empirical finding: identifying that diffusion-synthesized video anomalies exhibit spatiotemporal magnitude bias (inflated feature norms), which causes Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) models to overfit to magnitude shortcuts and underperform on subtle real anomalies.

Well-motivated technical contributions: the Class-Aware Pseudo-Anomaly Generator (CA-PAG) effectively anchors generation using CLIP-based seed selection and VLM prompt refinement, while the Domain-Aligned Regularized Module (DARM) successfully counteracts prototype collapse and feature norm discrepancies via domain alignment and usage-aware memory updates.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and strong results: the method achieves state-of-the-art results among methods that do not use real abnormal videos (e.g., 98.2% on ShanghaiTech, 82.5% on UCF-Crime, 95.1% on XD-Violence) and demonstrates impressive open-set generalization to unseen anomaly categories (Tables 8 and 9).

Detailed analysis and ablation studies: the paper provides thorough ablation of individual components (Table 5a), explicit quantification of feature norm changes before and after DARM (Table 5b), video generation fidelity metrics (Table 3), and sensitivity to the number of generated clips (Table 6).
weaknesses: Feature backbone disparity in baseline comparisons: PA-VAD uses features from a modern vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL 7B, 3,584-D), whereas most prior UVAD and WVAD baselines in Table 4 rely on standard I3D or C3D backbones. While Table 4 does evaluate baseline classifiers (Sultani et al., UR-DMU) on top of Qwen2.5-VL features within the authors' framework, it remains difficult to completely isolate whether the overall performance leap over prior published benchmarks stems from the synthetic data/DARM or the stronger multimodal pre-trained representation.

Reliance on heavy external foundation models: Although the approach completely avoids collecting real abnormal videos, it relies on extensive external knowledge and heavy generative models (Wan 2.2 14B diffusion model, Qwen3-30B VLM, Qwen2.5-VL 7B), requiring significant offline compute (e.g., ~55 hours on dual 96GB RTX 6000 Ada GPUs for UCF-Crime). Clearer discussion of this resource tradeoff compared to standard weakly supervised pipelines would strengthen the paper.

Underspecified details for pseudo-normal generation: While the generation of pseudo-abnormal clips is thoroughly documented, the paper mentions synthesizing 50–80 pseudo-normal clips for the domain alignment objective (Eq. 13) with relatively little explanation of the prompting strategy and conditioning used to generate these pseudo-normal samples.

strengths: Compelling and practical problem formulation: Training video anomaly detection without collecting real abnormal videos addresses a genuine bottleneck (cost, rarity, and privacy) in real-world deployment.

Insightful empirical analysis: The identification of the spatiotemporal magnitude bias—where diffusion synthesis artifacts produce abnormally large feature norms that hijack Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) top-k selection—is an important and well-supported observation (demonstrated across multiple backbones in Table 1 and Table 5b).

Principled and effective methodology: DARM effectively counters this bias by combining adversarial domain alignment on the normal stream with a usage-aware memory slot update rule, successfully preventing dominant high-magnitude prototypes from monopolizing representation learning.

Extensive experimental validation: The method achieves strong performance across three major benchmarks (ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, and XD-Violence), even surpassing real-abnormal WVAD baselines on ShanghaiTech and XD-Violence. The open-set evaluations (Tables 8 & 9) convincingly show that the model learns transferable abnormal cues rather than overfitting to synthetic artifacts.
weaknesses: Feature backbone disparity in benchmarking: The proposed detector is evaluated using frozen features extracted from Qwen2.5-VL 7B-Instruct (3,584-D), whereas most baseline comparisons in Table 4 rely on standard I3D or C3D backbones. While Table 1 confirms that magnitude bias exists across different backbones, it would be much more informative and fair to report the performance of baseline methods (e.g., UR-DMU and CMRL) using the exact same Qwen2.5-VL backbone.

Supervision ambiguity and dependence on anomaly vocabulary: Although the approach does not use real abnormal videos, it requires prior knowledge of target anomaly category names to drive CLIP seed selection and VLM prompt refinement. Clarifying how this setting positions itself relative to zero-shot/open-vocabulary VAD versus purely unsupervised VAD (UVAD) would improve clarity.

High computational and generative overhead: Generating the pseudo-anomaly datasets requires heavy generative foundation models (Wan 2.2 14B, Qwen3 30B, Qwen2.5-VL) and substantial compute (e.g., ~55 hours on two RTX 6000 Ada 96GB GPUs for UCF-Crime), which may hinder easy reproducibility and rapid iteration.

Under-specified generation protocol for pseudo-normal videos: While the paper mentions generating 50–80 pseudo-normal clips for the domain alignment loss, the exact prompting and seed selection procedures for these normal clips are less clearly detailed compared to the pseudo-abnormal pipeline.

strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: leveraging modern video diffusion models to synthesize pseudo-abnormal videos from only normal frames and class metadata, directly addressing the severe data scarcity and annotation bottleneck in weakly-supervised video anomaly detection (WVAD).

Well-designed generation pipeline (CA-PAG): combining CLIP-guided initial image retrieval with VLM-based scene-grounded prompt refinement effectively constrains the generative prior to produce surveillance-consistent, physically plausible anomaly videos.

Insightful diagnosis and technical remedy on the detection side (DARM): identifying that diffusion-synthesized videos suffer from inflated spatiotemporal feature magnitudes that bias MIL Top-k optimization, and successfully addressing this through domain alignment between real/pseudo normal distributions and usage-aware prototype memory updates.

Strong experimental results: achieves state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without real abnormal videos, outperforming UVAD baselines on both ShanghaiTech (+12.7% AUC over Seeker) and UCF-Crime (+1.9% AUC over MGSTRL), and even exceeding real-abnormal WVAD methods on ShanghaiTech (98.2% vs. 97.6%).

Detailed ablation studies that clearly substantiate the incremental utility of both the generation components (CLIP init, VLM refinement) and the detector regularizers (DA, usage-aware memory updates), along with sample efficiency analyses.
weaknesses: Prerequisite assumptions on anomaly categories: unlike classical UVAD which operates purely on normality without prior knowledge of anomaly types, PA-VAD assumes explicit textual knowledge of all target anomaly classes at training time to guide the diffusion generator. This nuance should be more clearly framed in the comparison with UVAD methods.

High computational requirement for pseudo-data synthesis: running Wan 2.2 (14B) requires a 100 GB GPU and roughly 9.5 minutes per 81-frame clip (~55 hours for UCF-Crime), which poses a non-trivial hardware barrier compared to standard VAD training pipelines.

Performance gap on complex, long-horizon anomalies: while effective on localized, motion-salient anomalies (e.g., fights, collisions), the approach still lags behind real-abnormal WVAD baselines on UCF-Crime (82.5% vs. 87.0%) due to the limitations of current video diffusion models in synthesizing prolonged, subtle, or context-heavy activities like shoplifting and vandalism.
Evaluation on additional diverse benchmarks: testing on other prominent VAD benchmarks such as XD-Violence or UCSD Ped2 would further strengthen the claims regarding cross-domain generalizability.

strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: Replacing scarce and costly real abnormal training videos with diffusion-synthesized pseudo-anomalies offers a practical and scalable paradigm for surveillance video anomaly detection.

Well-designed generation pipeline: The Class-Aware Pseudo-Anomaly Generator (CA-PAG) thoughtfully combines CLIP-based initial image retrieval with VLM-guided prompt refinement, ensuring that the generated anomalies are scene-consistent, visually grounded, and surveillance-appropriate.

Insightful problem identification and mitigation: Identifying the spatiotemporal magnitude bias (inflated feature norms in diffusion videos causing MIL top-k collapse) is an astute observation (Table 1). The proposed Domain-Aligned Regularized Module (DARM), featuring domain alignment and usage-aware memory updates, is well-targeted and effectively counters this artifact.

Solid empirical results on ShanghaiTech: Achieving 98.2% frame-level AUC without using any real abnormal videos is impressive, outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised methods and rivaling or exceeding top weakly supervised methods trained on real anomalies.

Clear ablation studies: The paper systematically evaluates each component (prompt refinement metrics in Table 3, module ablations in Table 5, and synthetic sample scaling in Table 6), demonstrating the individual contribution of both CA-PAG and DARM.
weaknesses: Conceptual ambiguity regarding the supervision setup: The authors characterize the setup as an 'unsupervised training regime' (Sec. 4.1) because no real abnormal videos are used. However, the pipeline requires explicit knowledge of the target abnormal class taxonomy (e.g., 'explosion', 'fighting', 'road accidents') and involves hand-crafted positive/negative prompt queries for CLIP image retrieval. Unlike genuine UVAD/OCC (one-class classification), which assumes zero prior knowledge of test anomaly types, this is fundamentally synthetic class-aware weakly supervised VAD. Clarifying this terminology would avoid overstating the 'unsupervised' nature of the method.

Limited open-world / out-of-vocabulary generalization: Because the memory bank and detector are optimized against a predefined closed set of anomaly categories, the model's resilience to unforeseen or out-of-vocabulary anomalies is unproven and warrants discussion or empirical testing.

Performance gap on complex surveillance datasets: While SHT results are very high, performance on UCF-Crime (82.5% AUC) falls significantly short of real-anomaly WVAD methods (~86.1–87.0%). Although the authors candidly note the difficulty of generating long-horizon, context-dependent actions, deeper exploration into how this gap could be narrowed would strengthen the work.

Heavy computational and memory requirements: The generation step relies on a 14B diffusion model running on an RTX 6000 Ada (utilizing ~96 GB VRAM) and requires 30–55 GPU hours just for video synthesis. Discussing the feasibility of using lighter or distilled video generators would improve practical utility.

Omission of pseudo-normal generation details: While the text specifies that 50 (SHT) and 80 (Crime) pseudo-normal clips were synthesized for domain alignment, the exact prompting strategy and init-selection criteria used for generating 'pseudo-normal' data are not clearly specified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, practical bottleneck in video anomaly detection: the scarcity and collection difficulty of real abnormal surveillance videos.

The overall pipeline is well-motivated and cohesive: combining CLIP-based seed frame retrieval with VLM prompt rewriting provides grounded visual anchors and prevents off-scene generative hallucinations in I2V diffusion.

The identification of feature norm inflation in diffusion-generated videos (Table 1) and its resulting bias in MIL Top-k instance selection is an insightful finding, effectively tackled by the Domain-Aligned Regularized Module (DARM).

Comprehensive experimental analysis, including component-wise ablations (Table 5), data scaling analysis (Table 6), and video generation fidelity metrics (Table 3), demonstrates clear benefits across ShanghaiTech and UCF-Crime.
weaknesses: The computational requirements for synthesis are quite heavy: running Wan 2.2 (14B) requires ~96 GB VRAM and roughly 55 hours of wall-clock time on a high-end RTX 6000 Ada GPU for UCF-Crime, which somewhat limits accessibility and reproducibility on standard research hardware.

While PA-VAD outperforms UVAD baselines, it relies on prior knowledge of target anomaly class names (e.g., 'Arson', 'Robbery') to prompt the VLM and generator, whereas typical UVAD methods are strictly open-ended and agnostic to target anomaly classes. The comparison to UVAD should more transparently qualify this distinction.

The generated clips are relatively short (81 frames, ~5 seconds at 16 fps), which limits the model's ability to represent multi-stage, temporally extended surveillance anomalies (e.g., subtle theft or shoplifting, as noted in the qualitative failure cases in Figure 10).
